Preparing a vaccination coverage survey

Source: vignettes/preparing-a-survey.Rmd
preparing-a-survey.Rmd
library(vaxsurvR)

Two things to describe

Before any data is touched, a survey needs two descriptions: the vaccination schedule it measures, and the mapping from its variable names to standardised concepts. Everything downstream reads those two objects, which is why no function in the package needs to know your form.

The schedule

A schedule is a table of doses and the chronological rules that make a recorded dose plausible.

schedule <- vcs_schedule(
  vaccine               = c("BCG", "PENTA1", "PENTA2", "PENTA3", "MCV1"),
  minimum_age_days      = c(0, 42, 70, 98, 270),
  maximum_age_days      = c(28, 76, 104, 132, 330),
  previous_dose         = c(NA, NA, "PENTA1", "PENTA2", NA),
  minimum_interval_days = c(NA, NA, 28, 28, NA)
)
schedule
#> <vcs_schedule: 5 dose(s), 3 antigen(s)>
#> # A tibble: 5 × 8
#>   vaccine antigen  dose label  minimum_age_days maximum_age_days previous_dose
#>   <chr>   <chr>   <int> <chr>             <dbl>            <dbl> <chr>        
#> 1 BCG     BCG         1 BCG                   0               28 NA           
#> 2 PENTA1  PENTA       1 PENTA1               42               76 NA           
#> 3 PENTA2  PENTA       2 PENTA2               70              104 PENTA1       
#> 4 PENTA3  PENTA       3 PENTA3               98              132 PENTA2       
#> 5 MCV1    MCV         1 MCV1                270              330 NA           
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: minimum_interval_days <dbl>

minimum_age_days and minimum_interval_days drive the data-quality checks; maximum_age_days drives timeliness only, and never invalidates a dose. Antigen and dose number are inferred from the names, so PENTA1, PENTA2 and PENTA3 become one series – which is what schedule_final_doses() and derive_fully_vaccinated() use.

schedule_final_doses(schedule)
#> [1] "BCG"    "PENTA3" "MCV1"

vcs_schedule_who() is a template covering the antigens most surveys measure. Adapt it to the national EPI calendar; it is a starting point, not a standard.

vcs_schedule_who(c("BCG", "PENTA1", "PENTA3", "MCV1"))
#> <vcs_schedule: 4 dose(s), 3 antigen(s)>
#> # A tibble: 4 × 8
#>   vaccine antigen  dose label  minimum_age_days maximum_age_days previous_dose
#>   <chr>   <chr>   <int> <chr>             <dbl>            <dbl> <chr>        
#> 1 BCG     BCG         1 BCG                   0               28 NA           
#> 2 PENTA1  PENTA       1 PENTA1               42               76 NA           
#> 3 PENTA3  PENTA       3 PENTA3               98              132 NA           
#> 4 MCV1    MCV         1 MCV1                270              330 NA           
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: minimum_interval_days <dbl>

The dictionary

A dictionary maps source variable names onto the concepts in vcs_concepts().

head(vcs_concepts(), 12)
#> # A tibble: 12 × 4
#>    concept      level     required description                                  
#>    <chr>        <chr>     <lgl>    <chr>                                        
#>  1 interview_id household TRUE     Unique identifier of the interview/submission
#>  2 household_id household TRUE     Household identifier                         
#>  3 child_id     child     TRUE     Child identifier (may be constructed)        
#>  4 caregiver_id child     FALSE    Caregiver/respondent identifier              
#>  5 psu          household TRUE     Primary sampling unit / cluster              
#>  6 segment      household FALSE    Segment within the PSU                       
#>  7 stratum      household FALSE    Sampling stratum                             
#>  8 weight       child     FALSE    Final sampling weight                        
#>  9 fpc          household FALSE    Finite population correction                 
#> 10 province     household FALSE    Administrative level 1                       
#> 11 district     household FALSE    Administrative level 2                       
#> 12 health_zone  household FALSE    Health zone (administrative level 3)

For a long-format export – one row per child – each concept is one column:

vcs_dictionary(
  child_id     = "childid",
  household_id = "hh_id",
  interview_id = "hh_id",
  psu          = "cluster",
  age_months   = "child_age_month",
  sex          = "child_sex"
)
#> <vcs_dictionary>
#>   repeats: 1 caregiver(s) x 1 child(ren)
#>   household level:
#>     interview_id -> hh_id
#>     household_id -> hh_id
#>     psu          -> cluster
#>   child level:
#>     child_id   -> childid
#>     age_months -> child_age_month
#>     sex        -> child_sex

Repeat groups in wide exports

Wide exports encode nesting in the column name: caregiver 1, child 2, vaccine 4 becomes something like CVH04_1_2. Dictionaries express that with placeholders:

Placeholder Meaning
{c} caregiver, or first-level repeat index
{k} child, or second-level repeat index
{v} vaccine index, unpadded
{vv} vaccine index, zero-padded to two digits
vaccine vaccine name from the schedule 
dict <- vcs_dictionary(
  interview_id  = "KEY",
  household_id  = "KEY",
  psu           = "psu_id",
  segment       = "segment_id",
  stratum       = "stratum",
  weight        = "final_weight",
  child_id      = "EC_ID_{c}_{k}",
  child_dob     = "EC_DOB_{c}_{k}",
  sex           = "EC_SEX_{c}_{k}",
  card_seen     = "CARD_{c}_{k}",
  card_status   = "CVH{vv}_{c}_{k}",
  card_date     = "CVH{vv}_date_{c}_{k}",
  recall_status = "VR{vv}_{c}_{k}",
  n_caregivers  = 2,
  n_children    = 2
)
dict
#> <vcs_dictionary>
#>   repeats: 2 caregiver(s) x 2 child(ren)
#>   household level:
#>     interview_id -> KEY
#>     household_id -> KEY
#>     psu          -> psu_id
#>     segment      -> segment_id
#>     stratum      -> stratum
#>   child level:
#>     child_id  -> EC_ID_{c}_{k}
#>     weight    -> final_weight
#>     child_dob -> EC_DOB_{c}_{k}
#>     sex       -> EC_SEX_{c}_{k}
#>     card_seen -> CARD_{c}_{k}
#>   vaccine level:
#>     card_status   -> CVH{vv}_{c}_{k}
#>     card_date     -> CVH{vv}_date_{c}_{k}
#>     recall_status -> VR{vv}_{c}_{k}

resolve_concept() shows exactly which source columns a mapping expands to, which is the quickest way to catch a typo before importing anything:

head(resolve_concept(dict, "card_date", schedule), 8)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 5
#>   concept   column         caregiver child vaccine
#>   <chr>     <chr>              <int> <int> <chr>  
#> 1 card_date CVH01_date_1_1         1     1 BCG    
#> 2 card_date CVH01_date_2_1         2     1 BCG    
#> 3 card_date CVH01_date_1_2         1     2 BCG    
#> 4 card_date CVH01_date_2_2         2     2 BCG    
#> 5 card_date CVH02_date_1_1         1     1 PENTA1 
#> 6 card_date CVH02_date_2_1         2     1 PENTA1 
#> 7 card_date CVH02_date_1_2         1     2 PENTA1 
#> 8 card_date CVH02_date_2_2         2     2 PENTA1

Coding conventions

Surveys code yes/no differently. The dictionary carries the convention, so no check has to guess.

vcs_dictionary(
  card_seen       = "CVH_card_shown",
  yes_values      = c("1", "Oui"),
  no_values       = c("2", "Non"),
  card_yes_values = c("1", "2")   # "yes, dated" and "yes, date incomplete"
)
#> <vcs_dictionary>
#>   repeats: 1 caregiver(s) x 1 child(ren)
#>   child level:
#>     card_seen -> CVH_card_shown

card_yes_values matters: many forms code a card-documented dose as 1 for “yes with date” and 2 for “yes, date illegible”, with 3 for “no” and 98 for “don’t know”. Values outside card_yes_values and outside the no/yes lists become NA rather than being read as a negative.

Keeping the dictionary in a spreadsheet

Survey teams usually maintain the mapping alongside the questionnaire.

tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(
  data.frame(
    concept = c("child_id", "psu", "card_status"),
    source  = c("EC_ID_{c}_{k}", "psu_id", "CVH{vv}_{c}_{k}")
  ),
  tmp, row.names = FALSE
)
read_vcs_dictionary(tmp, n_caregivers = 2, n_children = 2)
#> <vcs_dictionary>
#>   repeats: 2 caregiver(s) x 2 child(ren)
#>   household level:
#>     psu -> psu_id
#>   child level:
#>     child_id -> EC_ID_{c}_{k}
#>   vaccine level:
#>     card_status -> CVH{vv}_{c}_{k}
unlink(tmp)

Importing

read_vcs() reads everything as text by default. That is deliberate: letting R guess types is where a code like "01" silently becomes 1, and where a partial date "2025-03" becomes NA before anything has a chance to record that it was partial.

raw <- vcs_example_raw
dim(raw)
#> [1] 600 216
raw[1:3, c("KEY", "psu_id", "stratum", "final_weight")]
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   KEY         psu_id stratum final_weight
#>   <chr>       <chr>  <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 uuid:HH0001 PSU001 urban           1.53
#> 2 uuid:HH0002 PSU001 urban           1.53
#> 3 uuid:HH0003 PSU001 urban           1.46

read_surveycto() adds the defaults wide SurveyCTO exports need, including a warning when the delimiter looks mis-detected – a tab-separated file read as comma-separated parses to a single column, and it is better to be told.

Mapping 

mapped <- map_vcs_variables(vcs_example_raw, vcs_example_dictionary,
                            vcs_example_schedule)
mapped
#> <vcs_data>
#>   households  : 600
#>   children    : 256
#>   vaccinations: 3584 rows (14 vaccine[s])
#>   raw import  : 600 x 216 (preserved)
#>   source      : NA

A child record is created wherever any of its repeat-specific columns holds a value, so empty repeat slots do not become phantom children. Identifiers that are not mapped are constructed and marked as derived:

subset(derivation_rules(mapped), variable == "child_id")
#> # A tibble: 0 × 3
#> # ℹ 3 variables: table <chr>, variable <chr>, rule <chr>

strict = TRUE turns a missing source column into an error rather than a warning, which is what you want in a scheduled pipeline.

What to do next

Run validate_vcs() before anything else, and read vignette("data-quality").
